title: Measured Judgements: Hedging and Stance
canDo: Can express complex ideas with precise, measured stance and qualify claims fluently and without strain.
goal: State a view with appropriate hedging and sustain it in an extended discussion.

warmup.prompt: Post this topic: Is it fair to judge a society by its most successful citizens? Ask for an opening opinion in about 60 seconds.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak without interruption. Note two stance phrases for the wrap-up.

theory.structure: It could be argued that ... / To some extent, ... / There is a case for ... / Arguably, ...
examples: It could be argued that success reflects opportunity as much as effort.
To some extent, the criticism is justified, though it overlooks context.
Arguably, the problem lies less in the policy than in its execution.
theory.method: Show the hedges on screen with a strong claim and a hedged claim side by side. Ask guiding questions: What is the difference in certainty? When would a speaker choose each? Let the student restate their warm-up opinion with one hedge.
theory.checkQuestion: Which phrase shows the speaker is certain: arguably, or it is undeniable that?

comprehension.source: Read this editorial extract twice at native speed: Few would dispute that meritocracy is an appealing ideal. Yet the evidence suggests that privilege, far from being incidental, shapes which talents are ever recognised in the first place.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What do few people dispute? (meritocracy is an appealing ideal). What does the evidence suggest shapes recognition? (privilege).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: How does the writer signal the shift from the ideal to the critique? Ask the student to point to the word that marks the contrast, such as Yet.

conversation.task: Extended discussion: the student and the tutor debate the warm-up question for about twelve minutes. The student must use at least three hedges and must respond to two challenges from the tutor. Finish with a three-minute summary of the strongest point on each side.
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion. Take notes on minor errors silently, let the student lead, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: It is true that success is because of work.
Privilege is the reason for everything.

upgrades.accurate: It is true that success is because of work.
upgrades.native: To a large extent, success reflects sustained effort.

upgrades.accurate: Privilege is the reason for everything.
upgrades.native: Privilege plays a far larger role than is often acknowledged.

title: Emphasis and Focus: Cleft Sentences and Inversion
canDo: Can use advanced sentence structures for emphasis and organise information to highlight what matters most.
goal: Use cleft sentences and inversion to emphasise key points in speech and writing.

warmup.prompt: Post this topic: What is the most underrated skill in the modern workplace? Ask for an opening answer in about 60 seconds.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely. Note any structure they reach for to add emphasis.

theory.structure: It is X that ... / What I find striking is ... / Rarely have I ... / Not only ... but also ...
examples: It is listening that most managers neglect.
What I find striking is how little attention we pay to tone.
Rarely have I seen a team recover so quickly from a setback.
theory.method: Show a plain sentence and its emphatic version. Ask guiding questions: What is being highlighted? What is the new sentence order? Let the student rewrite one of their warm-up sentences with emphasis.
theory.checkQuestion: In Rarely have I seen a team recover, why does the auxiliary verb come before the subject?

comprehension.source: Read this column extract twice at native speed: Not only does the policy ignore regional differences, but it also assumes that every household can afford the upgrade. What the government calls reform is, in truth, a quiet transfer of cost.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What does the policy ignore? (regional differences). What does it assume about households? (they can afford the upgrade).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: How does the writer feel about the government's word reform? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the attitude, such as in truth.

conversation.task: Persuasive talk: the student argues a position on the warm-up topic in a three-minute monologue, then defends it against two challenges from the tutor. Each main point must use an emphatic structure at least once.
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion. Let the student lead, take silent notes on small errors, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: What I think is important is communication.
Rarely I have seen this happen.

upgrades.accurate: What I think is important is communication.
upgrades.native: What matters most is communication.

upgrades.accurate: Rarely I have seen this happen.
upgrades.native: Rarely have I seen this happen.

title: Industry Language: Business and Strategy Terms
canDo: Can use professional and industry-specific terminology accurately in a formal discussion.
goal: Discuss a business strategy using precise industry terms such as margin, stakeholder, and scalability.

warmup.prompt: Post this topic: What makes a start-up sustainable in the long run? Ask for an opening opinion in about 60 seconds.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely and note any industry terms they use or avoid.

theory.structure: Term + collocation in context (profit margin, stakeholder buy-in, scalable model, cash flow pressure)
examples: The company is protecting its profit margin by renegotiating supplier contracts.
Getting stakeholder buy-in early makes the strategy easier to deliver.
The model is scalable only if customer acquisition costs fall.
theory.method: Show each term with a collocation and a plain-English equivalent. Ask guiding questions: Would a plain word be less precise here? Let the student replace two plain words in their warm-up answer with industry terms.
theory.checkQuestion: Which term refers to the people with an interest in a decision: stakeholder or shareholder?

comprehension.source: Read this business news extract twice at native speed: The firm reported thinner margins this quarter, citing rising input costs. Analysts say that unless it can improve its scalability, investor confidence will remain fragile.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What did the firm report? (thinner margins). What is the cause? (rising input costs). What must improve? (scalability).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Are the analysts optimistic or cautious? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the attitude, such as remain fragile.

conversation.task: Strategy presentation: the student presents a short business strategy to the tutor, acting as a board member, and defends it against two questions about cost and stakeholder support. The student must use at least four industry terms naturally.
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion. Act as a demanding board member, take silent notes on terminology, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: The company has thin margins because it costs more.
We need the people who own shares to agree.

upgrades.accurate: The company has thin margins because it costs more.
upgrades.native: The company's margins are under pressure from rising input costs.

upgrades.accurate: We need the people who own shares to agree.
upgrades.native: We need shareholder buy-in before we proceed.

title: Irony and Understatement: Saying Less to Mean More
canDo: Can recognise and use irony, understatement, and sarcasm in speech, reading texts, and everyday conversation.
goal: Recognise and use understatement and irony in conversation, and explain the intended meaning.

warmup.prompt: Post this line: The printer has broken again, so today is going brilliantly. Ask: What is the speaker really saying?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student explain the irony in their own words, then ask one follow-up about the tone.

theory.structure: Understatement (not bad at all, a bit of a problem) and irony (positive words with a negative meaning), signalled by tone and context
examples: The project was a bit of a disaster. (The project failed badly.)
Well, that went brilliantly. (Things went badly.)
It is not the worst idea he has had. (It was a poor idea.)
theory.method: Show each example with its literal and intended meaning. Ask guiding questions: What is the literal meaning? What would a listener infer from the context? Let the student create one ironic remark about a common frustration.
theory.checkQuestion: If a speaker says the meeting went brilliantly after a terrible presentation, do they mean it literally?

comprehension.source: Play a short sarcastic exchange from a comedy clip, or read this text twice at native speed: Oh, wonderful. The train was cancelled again, so naturally we are all having a lovely walk home. Nothing says good planning like a bus that never arrives.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: Why are they walking home? (the train was cancelled). What does the speaker say about the bus? (it never arrives).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the speaker happy or annoyed? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the real feeling, such as Nothing says good planning.

conversation.task: Witty complaint: the tutor describes a minor everyday frustration (a late delivery, a noisy neighbour). The student responds using irony or understatement, then the tutor replies. Continue for five exchanges, shifting between light and serious tone.
phrases: That is not ideal, is it?
I suppose it could be worse.
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion. Act as a witty conversation partner, take silent notes on awkward phrasing, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: The day is very good because my printer broke.
That was a very bad presentation, I was very sad.

upgrades.accurate: The day is very good because my printer broke.
upgrades.native: Well, today is shaping up nicely.

upgrades.accurate: That was a very bad presentation, I was very sad.
upgrades.native: That presentation was a bit of a disaster.

title: Register Shifts: Formal and Casual in One Conversation
canDo: Can switch smoothly between casual chat and formal meetings, adapting vocabulary and tone to the audience.
goal: Move between casual and formal register in the same conversation without losing clarity.

warmup.prompt: Post this scenario: You meet a senior client at a casual lunch and the topic turns to a contract. Ask: How would you open the conversation?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student open in whichever register they choose, then ask them to shift to the other register.

theory.structure: Casual: to be fair, honestly, I'd say. Formal: with respect, I would contend, it would seem that. Shift with a signal phrase.
examples: Honestly, I think the deadline is unrealistic. (casual)
With respect, I would contend that the deadline is unrealistic. (formal)
To be fair, the team did its best, so let us review the timeline. (a bridge between the two)
theory.method: Show the same message in casual and formal versions. Ask guiding questions: Who is the audience? Which words signal the register? Let the student deliver one message in both registers.
theory.checkQuestion: Which word signals a formal register: honestly, or with respect?

comprehension.source: Read this short transcript twice at native speed: Look, I know it is a tight schedule. Still, with respect, the client expects a revised plan by Thursday, and I would contend that we can meet that if we prioritise the core features.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What does the client expect by Thursday? (a revised plan). What does the speaker think is needed? (prioritise core features).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Where does the speaker switch from casual to formal? Ask the student to point to the phrase that marks the shift, such as with respect.

conversation.task: Two-scene role-play: first the student and tutor chat casually about a weekend, then the conversation turns to a formal contract discussion. The student must make the shift at least twice and handle one interruption from the tutor in each register.
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion. Switch registers yourself without warning, take silent notes, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: Hey, with respect, I would be honest with you.
Dear boss, yeah I think it is a bit too much.

upgrades.accurate: Hey, with respect, I would be honest with you.
upgrades.native: Look, I would be candid with you, if I may.

upgrades.accurate: Dear boss, yeah I think it is a bit too much.
upgrades.native: Dear Ms Lee, I feel the workload is rather too heavy at present.

title: Persuasive Devices: Rhetoric in Speech
canDo: Can produce clear, well-structured, detailed speech on complex subjects, using rhetorical devices to persuade.
goal: Use rhetorical devices such as rhetorical questions, repetition, and contrast to persuade an audience.

warmup.prompt: Post this topic: Should public transport be free? Ask for a one-minute opening opinion.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely and note any rhetorical device they use naturally.

theory.structure: Rhetorical question + answer; repetition at the start of clauses (anaphora); contrast pairs (not X, but Y)
examples: Who really benefits from the status quo? Not the commuters.
We must invest in clean transport. We must invest in fair transport.
It is not about cost; it is about access.
theory.method: Show each device with an example and a label. Ask guiding questions: What effect does the repetition have? Who answers the rhetorical question? Let the student add one device to their warm-up opinion.
theory.checkQuestion: In a rhetorical question, does the speaker expect a real answer from the audience?

comprehension.source: Read this speech extract twice at native speed: Why do we accept delays as normal? Why do we tolerate overcrowded carriages? It is not inevitable. It is a choice, and it is one we can change.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What do we accept as normal? (delays). What does the speaker say about the choice? (it is one we can change).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the speaker resigned or determined? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the attitude, such as we can change.

conversation.task: Public address: the student gives a three-minute persuasive speech on the warm-up topic to the tutor, who acts as an audience member. The student must use at least two rhetorical devices, and the tutor asks two questions from the audience afterwards.
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion. Respond as a critical audience member, take silent notes on small errors, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: Why we accept the delays? It is normal.
It is not about money, is about people.

upgrades.accurate: Why we accept the delays? It is normal.
upgrades.native: Why do we accept delays as if they were normal?

upgrades.accurate: It is not about money, is about people.
upgrades.native: It is not about money; it is about people.

title: Cultural Subtext: Reading Between the Lines in Media
canDo: Can understand implicit meaning, cultural references, and subtle attitudes in fast-paced media and literature.
goal: Analyse the cultural subtext and implied meaning in a media text and explain it fluently.

warmup.prompt: Post this headline: Local council praises residents for their patience during the roadworks. Ask: What is the subtext here?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student explain the subtext freely, then ask what the headline is avoiding saying.

theory.structure: Euphemism and implicature: the surface meaning, the implied meaning, and the cultural reference that makes the implication work
examples: Residents showed remarkable patience. (The roadworks were a serious problem.)
The reform was described as bold. (Critics thought it was reckless.)
She is a safe pair of hands. (She is reliable, but not exciting.)
theory.method: Show each example with the surface and implied meaning. Ask guiding questions: What does the writer avoid saying? What does a reader need to know to understand the implication? Let the student decode one new example.
theory.checkQuestion: What is the implied meaning of describing a plan as bold in a newspaper column?

comprehension.source: Read this media column twice at native speed: The minister described the report as thorough, which in Westminster terms means nobody will read past the executive summary. The committee, meanwhile, has promised to look into it, a phrase that has preceded many quiet burials.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: How did the minister describe the report? (as thorough). What did the committee promise? (to look into it).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: How does the writer feel about the minister's words? Ask the student to decode the implied meaning of the phrase quiet burials and explain the cultural reference.

conversation.task: Media debate: the student and tutor discuss a current affairs topic chosen from a recent headline. The student must explain at least two implied meanings and the cultural context behind them, and respond to a challenge that the tutor raises.
phrases: The phrase carries the implication that ...
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion as an intellectual equal. Take silent notes on phrasing, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: The minister said the report is good, so it is good.
This phrase means they will look at it later.

upgrades.accurate: The minister said the report is good, so it is good.
upgrades.native: The minister praised the report, though the praise reads as a polite brush-off.

upgrades.accurate: This phrase means they will look at it later.
upgrades.native: The phrase is a familiar euphemism for shelving a report indefinitely.

title: Subtle Humour: Wit, Timing, and Self-Deprecation
canDo: Can use and understand subtle humour, wordplay, and self-deprecation in conversation with native-speed fluency.
goal: Use wit and self-deprecation naturally in conversation, and respond to humour from others.

warmup.prompt: Post this line: I am not saying I am bad at planning, but my calendar has never once been ready for me. Ask: Why is this funny?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student explain the humour, then ask them to add a line in the same style.

theory.structure: Understatement, self-deprecation, and callback (a joke that returns with a new twist)
examples: I am not saying I am disorganised, but my inbox has its own postcode.
I would love to help, but my schedule is currently a fiction.
As I said last week, the plan is perfect. The execution is a separate problem.
theory.method: Show each example and label the device. Ask guiding questions: What is the joke against? Who is the joke on? Let the student write one self-deprecating line about a small mistake they made recently.
theory.checkQuestion: In the inbox joke, is the speaker mocking someone else or themselves?

comprehension.source: Play a short comedy sketch with fast native dialogue, or read this text twice at native speed: My cooking is famous in my flat. Unfortunately, it is famous mostly for the smoke alarm, which has now learned my face and says hello.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What is the speaker famous for? (their cooking, or rather the smoke alarm). What has the alarm learned? (the speaker's face).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the speaker boasting or joking about their cooking? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the joke, such as famous mostly for the smoke alarm.

conversation.task: Witty exchange: the student and tutor trade light anecdotes about everyday failures, using self-deprecation and at least one callback to an earlier line. Keep the exchange natural and fast, and let the other speaker respond with a joke.
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion as a witty conversation partner. Match the student's pace, take silent notes on phrasing, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: I am not saying I am bad, but I am bad.
My cooking is very funny because the smoke is making a noise.

upgrades.accurate: I am not saying I am bad, but I am bad.
upgrades.native: I am not saying I am hopeless, but the evidence is against me.

upgrades.accurate: My cooking is very funny because the smoke is making a noise.
upgrades.native: My cooking is legendary, mostly because of the smoke alarm.

title: Nuanced Counter-Argument: Conceding and Rebutting
canDo: Can express complex ideas precisely, concede points fairly, and rebut arguments in a sophisticated way.
goal: Concede a valid point in a debate and rebut the rest with precise, sophisticated language.

warmup.prompt: Post this claim: Economic growth always improves people's lives. Ask: Where do you stand on this, and why?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student state a clear position in about 60 seconds, then challenge it with one counter-example.

theory.structure: While it is true that X, the more pressing issue is Y. / I take the point, though I would question the premise that ...
examples: While it is true that growth creates jobs, the more pressing issue is who captures the gains.
I take the point about productivity, though I would question the premise that wages follow automatically.
That may hold in aggregate, but it obscures considerable variation between regions.
theory.method: Show a weak rebuttal and a refined one side by side. Ask guiding questions: What does the concession signal? What is the rebuttal targeting: the premise or the conclusion? Let the student rebut one counter-point from the warm-up.
theory.checkQuestion: Does the phrase I take the point signal agreement, disagreement, or a partial concession?

comprehension.source: Read this editorial extract twice at native speed: Defenders of the scheme rightly point to the jobs it created. Their argument, however, rests on an assumption that the benefits were evenly shared, which the figures do not support.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What do defenders point to? (the jobs it created). What assumption does their argument rest on? (benefits were evenly shared).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the writer accept the defenders' argument? Ask the student to point to the words that show the concession and the rebuttal, such as rightly and however.

conversation.task: Structured debate: the student takes a side on the warm-up claim and debates the tutor for twelve minutes. Each turn, the student must make one concession and one rebuttal, using precise language.
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion as an intellectual equal. Take silent notes on phrasing, let the student lead, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: Yes it is true but I don't agree at all.
Economy is good, but the people are not happy.

upgrades.accurate: Yes it is true but I don't agree at all.
upgrades.native: While that is undeniably true, I would contest the conclusion.

upgrades.accurate: Economy is good, but the people are not happy.
upgrades.native: Growth is encouraging, but its benefits are unevenly distributed.

title: Native Choice: Refining Fluent Speech
canDo: Can express complex ideas without hesitation, with native-like word choice, collocation, and natural flow.
goal: Speak fluently on a complex topic and refine word choices toward natural, native-like collocations.

warmup.prompt: Post this topic: Is originality overrated in art and business? Ask for an immediate, detailed opening opinion.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak without interruption and note two collocations for the wrap-up.

theory.structure: Collocation and register: draw a conclusion, carry real weight, a sweeping generalisation, bear in mind, the bottom line
examples: We should be careful not to draw a sweeping conclusion from one case.
That point carries real weight, bearing in mind the evidence.
The bottom line is that originality depends on context.
theory.method: Show each collocation with a more textbook alternative. Ask guiding questions: Which version sounds more natural to a native speaker? Why? Let the student rebuild one of their warm-up sentences using a natural collocation.
theory.checkQuestion: Is it more natural to say draw a conclusion or make a conclusion in English?

comprehension.source: Read this essay extract twice at native speed: Originality is often treated as a virtue in itself. Yet most innovations are, on closer inspection, careful recombinations of existing ideas, and the bottom line is that context matters more than novelty.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: How is originality often treated? (as a virtue in itself). What do most innovations consist of? (careful recombinations of existing ideas).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the writer dismissive of originality or measured about it? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the balance, such as on closer inspection.

conversation.task: Fluent debate: the student and tutor discuss the warm-up topic at native speed for twelve minutes, shifting between formal and casual tone at least twice. The tutor finishes with a challenge to the student's central claim.
phrases: That carries real weight, bearing in mind ...
I would be wary of a sweeping generalisation about ...
conversation.mandate: Guide a high-level discussion as a native-level coach. Take silent notes on word choice, let the student lead, and keep the speaking share at 90 percent or more.

mistakes: We should not make a big conclusion from one case.
The most important thing at the end is that context is important.

upgrades.accurate: We should not make a big conclusion from one case.
upgrades.native: We should not draw a sweeping conclusion from a single case.

upgrades.accurate: The most important thing at the end is that context is important.
upgrades.native: The bottom line is that context matters.
